guides.title: If a Fire Starts at Home
guides.description: How to get out quickly and safely when there is a fire in your home.
steps: Alert everyone in the home and get out immediately. Do not stop to collect belongings.
Use your escape plan. If there is smoke, stay low and crawl under it toward the exit.
Before opening a closed door, feel it with the back of your hand. If it is hot, use another way out.
If you open a door, open it slowly and be ready to shut it quickly if heavy smoke or fire is present.
Close doors behind you as you leave to help slow the spread of fire and smoke.
Go to your agreed meeting place outside, then call your local emergency number from outside the building.
Stay outside. If someone is still inside, tell the firefighters right away.
thingsToDo: Get out first, then call for help.
Crawl low under smoke.
Meet at a planned spot outside so everyone can be counted.
If your clothes catch fire: stop, drop to the ground and roll to smother the flames.
thingsToAvoid: Do not go back inside for people, pets or belongings.
Do not open a door that feels hot.
Do not use lifts/elevators during a fire.
Do not hide in a closet or under a bed.

guides.title: Smoke Alarms and Escape Planning
guides.description: Prepare your home so everyone can escape a fire in time.
steps: Install smoke alarms on every level of your home, inside every bedroom and outside sleeping areas.
Test your smoke alarms regularly and replace batteries when needed.
Replace the whole smoke alarm unit every 10 years, or as the manufacturer says.
Draw a written escape plan that shows two ways out of every room.
Choose a meeting place outside the home.
Practice your escape plan at least twice a year, at different times of the day and night.
Aim to get everyone out in under 2 minutes.
thingsToDo: Make sure everyone, including children and guests, knows the plan.
Plan extra help for babies, older adults and people with disabilities.
Keep exits and escape routes clear.
Contact your local fire service if you cannot afford or install a smoke alarm.
thingsToAvoid: Do not disable smoke alarms while cooking.
Do not leave cooking unattended.
Do not block doors or windows with furniture.
guides.sourceName: Ready.gov - Practice Your Home Fire Escape Plan

guides.title: Before and During a Flood
guides.description: Stay out of flood water and move to safety when a flood threatens.
steps: Listen to local alerts, radio or authorities for flood information and instructions.
Evacuate immediately if you are told to do so.
If you are not told to evacuate, move to higher ground or a higher floor of the building.
Do not walk, swim or drive through flood waters. Turn Around, Don't Drown!
Stay off bridges over fast-moving water.
If you are trapped by moving water, move to the highest possible point and call your local emergency number.
thingsToDo: Prepare an emergency kit with water, a first aid kit, a flashlight and batteries.
Keep important papers in a safe place away from possible flooding.
Know the flood risk in your area and your evacuation route.
Let family and important contacts know you are safe.
thingsToAvoid: Do not drive around road barriers or into flooded roads.
Do not become trapped in a basement or attic.
Do not go into a flooded room if water may touch electrical outlets or cords.

guides.title: After a Flood
guides.description: Return home and clean up safely once flood waters have gone down.
steps: Return home only when local authorities say it is safe.
Avoid contact with flood water. It may be contaminated with sewage or chemicals.
If you touch flood water, wash thoroughly with soap and clean water.
Do not enter a flooded room if water may be touching electrical outlets, appliances or cords.
Have any electrical appliance that got wet checked by a professional before using it.
Wear protective clothing and sturdy shoes during clean-up.
Take photographs of damage for insurance or relief claims.
thingsToDo: Scrub surfaces with detergent and water, and dry the area quickly to limit mould.
Tell family and friends that you are safe.
Throw away food that touched flood water.
thingsToAvoid: Do not turn off the power at the breaker box if you must stand in water to reach it.
Do not mix cleaning products such as bleach and ammonia.
Do not walk or drive through standing water, especially if power lines may be down.

guides.title: During an Earthquake: Drop, Cover, Hold On
guides.description: The recommended action to protect yourself while the ground is shaking.
steps: DROP to your hands and knees so the shaking cannot knock you over.
COVER your head and neck with your arms. If a sturdy desk or table is nearby, crawl under it.
HOLD ON to your shelter and stay covered until the shaking stops.
If your shelter moves, move with it.
If you are in bed, stay there and protect your head and neck with a pillow.
If you are outside, move away from buildings, trees, streetlights and power lines, then drop, cover and hold on.
If you use a wheelchair or walker, lock the wheels or brakes and protect your head and neck.
thingsToDo: Practice Drop, Cover, Hold On with your family.
Stay inside until the shaking stops.
Protect your head and neck even if you cannot reach a table.
thingsToAvoid: Do not run outside while the ground is shaking.
Do not stand in a doorway.
Stay away from windows, mirrors, hanging objects and tall furniture.

guides.title: After an Earthquake
guides.description: Stay safe from aftershocks, fires and damaged buildings.
steps: Expect aftershocks. If one happens, Drop, Cover and Hold On again.
Check yourself and the people around you for injuries and give first aid if you can.
Look for small fires and put them out if it is safe. Fire is a common hazard after an earthquake.
Open cabinets carefully because objects can fall off shelves.
Wear sturdy shoes, long sleeves and gloves when moving around debris.
Listen to the radio or local alerts for instructions.
If you live near the coast and the shaking was strong, move to higher ground in case of a tsunami.
thingsToDo: Follow instructions from local authorities.
If you smell gas or hear hissing and suspect a leak, leave the building and report it from outside.
Leave a damaged building and stay out until it is declared safe.
thingsToAvoid: Do not use matches, lighters or electrical switches if you smell gas.
Do not walk barefoot around broken glass.
Do not re-enter damaged buildings.

guides.title: If You Are in a Road Accident
guides.description: Immediate steps to take after a crash.
steps: Stay calm and take a few slow breaths before you act.
Check yourself, your passengers and others nearby for injuries.
Call your local emergency number straight away if anyone is hurt, airbags opened or the vehicle cannot be driven.
If the crash is minor and it is safe, move the vehicle off the road. Do not move it if someone is hurt or trapped.
Turn on hazard lights and place a warning triangle if you have one. Step away from traffic.
If you cannot get out safely, stay buckled in with hazard lights on and wait for help.
Exchange names, phone numbers, vehicle details and insurance details with the other driver.
Take photos of the scene and note witness contact details.
thingsToDo: Stay on the line with the emergency operator until they tell you to hang up.
See a doctor afterwards if you have pain, dizziness or headaches.
thingsToAvoid: Never leave the scene of an accident.
Do not stand in traffic lanes.
Do not argue about who is at fault at the scene.
guides.sourceName: KidsHealth (Nemours) - What to Do After a Car Crash

guides.title: Helping Injured People at a Crash
guides.description: How to help without putting yourself or the injured at greater risk.
steps: Make sure the scene is safe for you first. Park well away, turn on hazard lights and watch for traffic.
Call your local emergency number or ask someone nearby to call. Give the exact location and the number of injured people.
Do not move injured people unless there is immediate danger such as fire.
If someone is bleeding heavily, press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth.
Talk calmly to the injured person and tell them help is coming.
Stay with them until the emergency services arrive and tell responders what you saw.
thingsToDo: Keep injured people still and warm.
Follow the instructions of the emergency operator.
Learn first aid through an approved course.
thingsToAvoid: Do not remove a motorcyclist's helmet unless they cannot breathe and you are trained.
Do not give food or drink to injured people.
Do not put yourself in the path of traffic.

guides.title: Severe Bleeding
guides.description: Control heavy bleeding until medical help arrives.
steps: Call your local emergency number or ask someone else to call.
Protect yourself: use gloves or a plastic bag if available.
Press firmly and directly on the wound with a clean cloth or dressing.
Keep pressing. If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top and keep pressing.
If the bleeding on an arm or leg is life-threatening and does not stop, and you have a tourniquet and training, apply it.
Keep the person lying down and warm until help arrives.
thingsToDo: Keep pressure on the wound without stopping.
Wash your hands after giving first aid.
Take a Stop the Bleed or first aid course to learn the skills properly.
thingsToAvoid: Do not remove cloths that are soaked. Add more on top.
Do not remove objects stuck in a wound.
Do not leave the person alone.
guides.sourceName: Stop the Bleed (American College of Surgeons)

guides.title: Minor Burns
guides.description: First aid for small burns from heat, hot liquid or steam.
steps: Move the person away from the source of the burn.
Cool the burn right away with cool, running water (not ice cold) for 10 to 20 minutes.
Gently remove rings, watches or tight items near the burn before swelling starts.
Cover the burn loosely with a clean, non-stick or sterile dressing.
Seek medical help if the burn is large, deep, on the face, hands, feet or genitals, or caused by chemicals or electricity.
thingsToDo: Keep the burned area clean and covered.
Get medical advice for any burn you are unsure about.
thingsToAvoid: Do not use ice, butter, oil or toothpaste on a burn.
Do not break blisters.
Do not remove clothing that is stuck to the burn.

guides.title: Choking (Conscious Adult)
guides.description: Help an adult who cannot cough, speak or breathe because of something stuck in the throat.
steps: Check that the person is really choking: they cannot cough, speak or breathe. Ask if you can help.
Lean the person forward and give 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades.
If that does not clear the blockage, give 5 abdominal thrusts.
Keep alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object comes out or the person can breathe.
If the person becomes unresponsive, call your local emergency number and start CPR.
thingsToDo: Call for emergency help if the blockage does not clear quickly.
Have the person checked by a doctor afterwards.
Infants need a different technique, so learn it in an approved first aid course.
thingsToAvoid: Do not slap the back of someone who is coughing strongly. Let them keep coughing.
Do not put fingers in the mouth blindly.
Do not give water to someone who is choking.

guides.title: Hands-Only CPR (Adult)
guides.description: What to do for an adult who suddenly collapses and is not breathing normally.
steps: Check the scene is safe. Tap the person's shoulders and shout to see if they respond.
If there is no response and no normal breathing, call your local emergency number or ask someone to call and to bring an AED.
Place the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest and your other hand on top.
Push hard and fast: about 5 cm (2 inches) deep at a rate of 100 to 120 pushes per minute.
Let the chest rise fully between pushes.
Continue until emergency responders arrive, an AED is ready or the person starts to move.
If an AED arrives, turn it on and follow its spoken instructions.
thingsToDo: Push without stopping. Do not worry about being perfect.
Take turns if someone else can help, because pushing is tiring.
Take a certified CPR course to learn the full technique, including children and rescue breaths.
thingsToAvoid: Do not stop pushing unless help takes over or the person wakes up.
Do not delay calling for help.
Do not move the person unless they are in danger.

guides.title: Someone Receives an Electric Shock
guides.description: Help a person who may still be in contact with electricity, without becoming a victim yourself.
steps: Look first. Do not touch the person: they may still be in contact with the electricity and the current could pass through you.
Call your local emergency number or have someone else call.
Turn off the power at the main switch or unplug the appliance, but only if it is safe to do so.
Once the person is free of the electrical source, check if they are breathing.
If they are not breathing normally, start CPR (see the Hands-Only CPR guide).
Cover the person lightly and keep them warm until help arrives.
Everyone who has had an electric shock should be seen by a doctor, even if they feel fine.
thingsToDo: Keep your distance until the power is off.
Tell the emergency operator it was an electrical injury.
Remember that electric shock can cause burns inside the body.
thingsToAvoid: Do not touch the person or the electrical source while power is on.
Do not touch burns, break blisters or remove burned clothing.
Do not use water near the electrical source.
guides.sourceName: CDC - Protect Yourself From Electrical Hazards

guides.title: Electrical Safety and Downed Power Lines
guides.description: Prevent electrical accidents at home and stay away from fallen power lines.
steps: Never touch a fallen power line. Treat every downed line as live.
Stay at least 10 feet (3 metres) away from overhead power lines and anything touching them.
Call the power company and your local emergency number to report the downed line.
Do not drive through standing water if downed power lines may be in the water.
Have any electrical appliance that has been in contact with water checked by a professional before using it.
thingsToDo: Keep electrical appliances and cords away from water.
Replace damaged cords and plugs.
Turn off and unplug a faulty appliance if it is safe to do so.
thingsToAvoid: Do not touch electrical equipment with wet hands.
Do not overload sockets or extension cords.
Do not enter a flooded room if water covers electrical outlets or cords.
guides.sourceName: CDC - Protect Yourself From Electrical Hazards

tips.text: Practice your home fire escape plan at least twice a year, at different times of day.
Put smoke alarms inside every bedroom, outside sleeping areas and on every level of your home.
If you are escaping a fire and there is smoke, stay low and crawl to the exit.
Turn Around, Don't Drown! Never walk, swim or drive through flood water.
Keep important papers in a safe place away from possible flooding.
Stay off bridges over fast-moving water.
When the ground shakes: Drop, Cover, and Hold On.
Practice Drop, Cover, Hold On with your family so everyone reacts quickly.
Expect aftershocks after an earthquake and be ready to Drop, Cover and Hold On again.
After a crash, check for injuries first and call emergency services if anyone is hurt.
Turn on your hazard lights and step away from traffic after a crash if it is safe.
For severe bleeding, press firmly and directly on the wound with a clean cloth and keep pressing.
Cool a minor burn with cool running water for 10 to 20 minutes. Do not use ice.
Take a first aid and CPR course. Trained helpers save lives.
Never touch a fallen power line. Stay at least 10 feet (3 metres) away and report it.
Keep electrical appliances and cords away from water, and never touch them with wet hands.
